security_spec.violation_condition: XiangShan is an RV64 processor; ADDD/SUBD are RV32-only P-extension instructions encoded in the OP-IMM-32 (instr[6:0]=0x1B) opcode space with funct3=0x6. If the XiangShan decoder (DecodeUnit.scala:791) lacks explicit illegal-instruction trapping for OP-IMM-32 funct3=0x6 encodings, these bit patterns will fall through to the decodeDefault path. However, the register-pair format (rd_p/rs1_p/rs2_p as 4-bit indices selecting X[2*p] and X[2*p+1]) reinterprets standard RISC-V register fields: rd_p uses only instr[11:8] (vs standard instr[11:7]), rs1_p uses instr[19:16] (vs instr[19:15]), rs2_p uses instr[24:21] (vs instr[24:20]). A decoder bug that maps these pair-indices onto standard 5-bit register specifiers would read/write wrong architectural registers, silently corrupting register state. The encoding forces instr[7]=0 (the 8-bit opcode byte is exactly 0x1B), imposing a constraint on what is normally RD[0] in standard encodings — failure to validate instr[7]==0 would accept invalid encoding variants.
security_spec.summary: RV32-only ADDD/SUBD instructions reuse OP-IMM-32 opcode with funct3=0x6 and register-pair format (4-bit rd_p/rs1_p/rs2_p indices); XiangShan RV64 decoder must trap these as illegal, and any future implementation must correctly decode pair-indices from truncated register bit-fields to avoid silent register file corruption

findings.finding: No P-extension decode table exists in the decode_table assembly. XDecode, FpDecode, BitmanipDecode, ScalarCryptoDecode, VecDecoder, ZicondDecode, ZimopDecode, ZfaDecode, and others are included, but no P-ext table. Any ADDD/SUBD encoding (OP-IMM-32 funct3=0x6) that hits the decoder will receive decodeDefault -> SelImm.INVALID_INSTR -> exceptionII -> illegalInstr trap. This is correct behavior for an RV64 core that does not implement P-extension.
findings.snippet:
val decode_table: Array[(BitPat, List[BitPat])] = XDecode.table ++
    FpDecode.table ++
    BitmanipDecode.table ++
    ScalarCryptoDecode.table ++
    ...
    ZfaDecode.table

findings.finding: decodeDefault correctly maps all unmatched instruction BitPat encodings to SelImm.INVALID_INSTR, which is subsequently detected by exceptionII (line 878: decodedInst.selImm === SelImm.INVALID_INSTR). This is the safety net for any undefined encoding in the OP-IMM-32 (0x1B) space including funct3=0x6 (ADDD/SUBD).
findings.snippet:
def decodeDefault: List[BitPat] =
    List(SrcType.X, SrcType.X, SrcType.X, FuType.X, FuOpType.X, N, N, N, N, N, N, N, UopSplitType.X, SelImm.INVALID_INSTR)

findings.finding: The primary illegal-instruction gate correctly triggers on SelImm.INVALID_INSTR. For OP-IMM-32 funct3=0x6 encodings, no decode table entry matches, so decodeDefault supplies INVALID_INSTR, and exceptionII fires. The decodedInst.exceptionVec(illegalInstr) is then asserted at line 915.

XDecode defines only ADDIW (funct3=0x0), SLLIW (funct3=0x1), SRAIW/SRLIW (funct3=0x5) in the OP-IMM-32 (0x1B) opcode space. Funct3 values 0x2-0x4 and 0x6-0x7 have no entries and fall through to decodeDefault -> illegal. ADDD/SUBD at funct3=0x6 is correctly absent, causing a trap rather than silent decode to an unintended execution path.
findings.snippet:
ADDIW   -> XSDecode(SrcType.reg, SrcType.imm, SrcType.X, FuType.alu, ALUOpType.addw, SelImm.IMM_I, xWen = T, canRobCompress = T),
    SLLIW   -> XSDecode(SrcType.reg, SrcType.imm, SrcType.X, FuType.alu, ALUOpType.sllw, SelImm.IMM_I, xWen = T, canRobCompress = T),
    SRAIW   -> XSDecode(SrcType.reg, SrcType.imm, SrcType.X, FuType.alu, ALUOpType.sraw, SelImm.IMM_I, xWen = T, canRobCompress = T),
    SRLIW   -> XSDecode(SrcType.reg, SrcType.imm, SrcType.X, FuType.alu, ALUOpType.srlw, SelImm.IMM_I, xWen = T, canRobCompress = T),

findings.finding: Register operand extraction uses standard 5-bit RISC-V fields: inst.RS1 (19,15), inst.RS2 (24,20), inst.RD (11,7). There is no rd_p/rs1_p/rs2_p 4-bit register-pair index logic anywhere in XiangShan. Even if ADDD/SUBD encodings were somehow decoded (which they are not, blocked by decodeDefault), the standard field extraction would read the wrong sub-fields (e.g., instr[11:7]=RD 5-bit instead of rd_p instr[11:8]=4-bit). This is moot because the instruction is always trapped first.
findings.snippet:
decodedInst.lsrc(0) := inst.RS1
  decodedInst.lsrc(1) := inst.RS2
  decodedInst.lsrc(2) := Mux(isFMA, inst.FS3, inst.VD)
  decodedInst.lsrc(3) := V0_IDX.U
  decodedInst.ldest := inst.RD

findings.finding: The misa.P bit (bit 15) is hardwired to 0 at reset, correctly advertising that packed-SIMD (P-extension) is not implemented. This provides a software-visible gate: any OS or hypervisor checking misa.P before using P-ext instructions will see they are unavailable.
findings.snippet: val P = RO(15).withReset(0.U).withDescription("Tentatively reserved packed-SIMD extension bit.")

findings.finding: OP_IMM_32 is defined as 'b00_110' (instr[6:2]=0x06, instr[6:0]=0x1B), matching the RISC-V spec encoding. The decoder correctly classifies instructions in this opcode space.

DecodeUnitConstants defines standard 5-bit register field boundaries: RD(11,7), RS1(19,15), RS2(24,20). These match the standard RISC-V base ISA. No P-extension register-pair field definitions (rd_p[11:8], rs1_p[19:16], rs2_p[24:21]) exist, which is correct since P-ext is not implemented.
findings.snippet:
val RD_MSB  = 11
    val RD_LSB  = 7
    val RS1_MSB = 19
    val RS1_LSB = 15
    val RS2_MSB = 24
    val RS2_LSB = 20
